quote: so I wasn't sure if it's a scam.
stewart_read: Customer directly names the scam concern but the rep's intro at 00:05 never anchored company legitimacy (no mention of licensing, certification, or lead source specificity) before this came up.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged the program explanation sufficient reassurance, but the customer's word choice ('scam') needed a direct answer, not a pivot to mechanics.
coaching_implication: Add a specific legitimacy anchor ('we're a licensed installer, this came from your request on X') before or immediately after the scam question, rather than moving straight to program details.

quote: I'm an electrician, and one of my, coworkers does solar.
stewart_read: Customer discloses relevant background and implicit prior exposure to solar; rep says 'Okay. Awesome.' and moves straight to bill collection without asking what the coworker's system looks like or what he already knows.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may be intentionally staying in setter scope and avoiding a technical debate with someone who claims expertise — a defensible scope discipline move.
coaching_implication: A quick probe ('what does your coworker's setup look like?') could have surfaced objections or interest depth without creating scope creep.

quote: But I don't have that stuff with me, so I'll have to call back.
stewart_read: This is a classic soft deferral objection; rep accepts it with an alternative (text) but never locks a callback time or appointment.
coaching_implication: Rep should have proposed a specific day/time to follow up rather than leaving 'call back' undefined.

quote: Okay. Yeah. No problem. I could send you a text as well.
stewart_read: Button-up is reduced to a vague text promise with no date, no time, no verbal handshake ('is that fair?'), and no appointment.
coaching_implication: Even without the bill, rep could have booked a tentative appointment time contingent on receiving the bill, per bill_collection lead-type flexibility.

quote: How's it going today? Yeah. I was just honestly asking if it's,
stewart_read: Customer's first reply jumps straight past rapport into suspicion; rep never states how the lead was generated (form fill, referral) to preempt this.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep's opening at 00:05 did reference 'a request' for solar info, so some legitimacy grounding existed, but it wasn't specific enough to preempt the scam question that followed seconds later.
coaching_implication: Be more specific about lead source ('you filled out a form on our site about solar') to close the legitimacy gap before it becomes a direct scam accusation.

quote: I'm pretty familiar with it. Oh, there you go.
stewart_read: Customer self-identifies as knowledgeable (electrician, solar-adjacent trade contact) — a qualified, informed lead signal the rep doesn't leverage into deeper interest capture.
coaching_implication: Use trade knowledge as a hook: ask what convinced/didn't convince him about his coworker's system to build curiosity toward his own numbers.

quote: we could definitely kinda crush the numbers here, kinda see what it looks like for you
stewart_read: Rep's pitch is loaded with 'kinda' and 'yeah' softeners across this segment, undercutting authority on a customer already questioning legitimacy.
coaching_implication: Tighten language into declarative statements when addressing a skeptical customer — softeners read as uncertainty, not reassurance.
